messages.author: 8483ab0cfd573506
messages.subject: theme_<journal_name> library
parts:
Hi All,

Working in research, like I'm sure a reasonable number of others do, I
have to produce graphs for journals. When it's for a powerpoint
presentation or email for discussion among colleagues, graphics are
easy, but when you have the journals strict specifications (this may
be my lack of skills) tweaking everything can be a right pain, and
consume hours.

Using my recent experiences as examples, some journals have 2.2 inch
columns (3 col) others 8.6cm columns (2col). Of course producing
graphs for these requires quite different settings, font sizes, point
sizes, line widths, axis tick mark lengths etc.

This may have been floated before, but would others find value in
having an (unofficial) theme database for journals, where users can
contribute the themes they set up?

In the same way endnote has gone from having APA and Harvard styles
(think theme_grey and theme_bw) to having almost all journals custom
bib formats listed, we could have theme_nature theme_stroke
theme_microbiology etc.

I have more thoughts on this but figure that's enough to gauge the
response.

Cheers

A start on this is the theme gallery at
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Themes There are not any journal
specific themes there, but there is no reason there couldn't be.

If it were to get bigger, a separate package of just themes would be the
way to go. That is not something that should be coupled to the ggplot2
release cycle.

messages.author: 8b78a79c64716511
messages.subject: Re: theme_<journal_name> library
parts:
Hey there,

I started making related adjustments with theme_minimal from the github page for myself, too.  I had to tweak a couple of lines in theme_minimal to get it to play nicely with version 0.9.0 - for some reason at the time I used it, I think I had to switch the units for axis.ticks.length and axis.ticks.margin from "lines" to "cm".

Other than that, I have generally been saving plots using the journal's requested final dimensions, and you'll note that fonts, font sizes and line sizes should remain appropriate if you do that (because base.size is set at 12 and the default sans serif font is Helvetica).  Using ggplot2 for this has saved me a lot of those painful hours, especially when I have to go back and change something in the original dataset and analysis for some reason (which inevitably happens) - my plots are basically publication-ready by the point where I use ggsave().

Here's my tweaked version of theme_minimal, which might be really close to what you'd want.  Also remember to use theme_get() (no argument) to see the settings of the current plot in the quartz window in case there's a fiddly bit that you want to fiddle with.  I agree with Brian - themes are going to get tweaked more frequently than ggplot2 itself, so the github page seems like a logical place to keep updated and expanded themes.

   theme_minimal <- function (base_size = 12, base_family = "")
     {
         structure(list(axis.line = theme_segment(),
                        axis.text.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, lineheight = 0.9, vjust = 1, colour="black"),
                        axis.text.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, lineheight = 0.9, hjust = 1, colour="black"),
                        axis.ticks = theme_segment(colour = "black"),
                        axis.title.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size, vjust = -0.5, hjust=0.5),
                        axis.title.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size, angle = 90, vjust = 0.2),
                        axis.ticks.length = unit(0.15, "cm"),
                        axis.ticks.margin = unit(0.1, "cm"),
                        legend.background = theme_rect(colour = NA),
                        legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA),
                        legend.key.size = unit(1.2, "lines"),
                        legend.key.height = NULL,
                        legend.key.width = NULL,
                        legend.text = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8),
                        legend.text.align = NULL,
                        legend.title = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
                        legend.title.align = NULL,
                        legend.position = "right",
                        legend.direction = NULL,
                        legend.box = NULL,
                        panel.background = theme_blank(),
                        panel.border = theme_blank(),
                        panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
                        panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
                        panel.margin = unit(0.25, "lines"),
                        strip.background = theme_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
                        strip.text.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8),
                        strip.text.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, angle = -90),
                        plot.background = theme_blank(),
                        plot.title = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 1.2),
                        plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1, 0.5, 0.5), "lines")),
                  class = "options")
     }

messages.author: a3c668b849637905
messages.subject: Re: theme_<journal_name> library
parts:
There has been some discussion on this mailing list, but the outcome
is usually that very few people do share their themes. The examples on
the wiki are probably a start, but it would be nice to expand the
collection, share ideas to converge towards elegant and well-thought
designs, and perhaps use the feedback to fine-tune the choice of
default themes included in ggplot2 too:

- maybe some default themes could use minor tweaks. For instance I
find the strip background of theme_bw() too heavy; I almost always
change it to something lighter or even white. That's in fact the main
reason I wrote my version of theme_minimal()

- theme_minimal() or some version of it seems quite popular, as well
as theme_fullpage() (no margins). Maybe these two could be included in
the main package instead of seeing multiple versions being posted in
different places (and sometimes lacking proper updates)?

- there was some discussion on whether the modifyList() approach could
become the default definition of a new theme, all based on
theme_grey() maybe. I'm not sure where this idea was left in the end.
The basic design of themes is still a subject of debate every now and
then, I'm not sure a completely satisfying design has been agreed
upon.

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: theme_<journal_name> library
parts:
Thanks for the feedback.

Would either of you three like to discuss this further and work
together to get something that we could look to circulate to a wider
group for feedback and potential implementation?

I'm thinking we would basically need a 'cover all' type template that
people can grab, plug in/tweak the options so it is at a point where
the plot can be created with no inline adjustments, and then can be
uploaded (somewhere).

I'm happy to pursue on my own, I know I'd miss a few things though so
would prefer to have the 'template/step by step guide' a bit tighter
before circulating.

messages.author: a3c668b849637905
messages.subject: Re: theme_<journal_name> library
parts:
I too think the ggplot2-dev mailing list is a good place to discuss
these developments. There are some open questions, I think, regarding
the scope and design of themes in ggplot2 that might influence the
rest of the package. For instance:

- Should themes include the ability to set default scales? (e.g range
of line widths and sizes, default colour scales). Default layer
aesthetic settings? (e.g if your theme has a black background, it
would make sense that, say, geom_text layers use a white colour by
default to be visible.

- What is the best data structure for themes? On one end, it should
have a tree-like inheritance where children share defaut settings from
parents (axis tick marks have by default the same colour as axis
lines, for example). At the other end, it should also allow setting a
maximum level of details, still keeping a fairly concise yet explicit
syntax (nested nested lists quickly become painful to write/modify).

(There are a few previous discussions on this list and github.)

Best,

baptiste
